params.question: Cellulose and glycogen are both polysaccharides made of glucose. Why can humans digest glycogen but not cellulose?

answers.text: Cellulose is insoluble in water, preventing digestive enzymes from accessing it

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Solubility is not the critical factor. Cellulose resists digestion because it contains a type of glycosidic bond (beta-1,4) that human digestive enzymes cannot cleave. Glycogen has alpha-1,4 bonds that amylase readily hydrolyses.

answers.text: Glycogen chains are shorter than cellulose chains and therefore easier to break down

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chain length is not the deciding factor — glycogen molecules are actually very large. The key difference is the type of glycosidic bond: alpha bonds in glycogen are digestible, while the beta bonds in cellulose are not, because humans lack the enzyme cellulase.

answers.text: Cellulose contains a glycosidic bond that human digestive enzymes cannot cleave

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Cellulose has beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds, and humans lack the enzyme cellulase to break them. Glycogen has alpha-1,4 bonds that pancreatic and salivary amylase readily hydrolyse. This is why cellulose passes through the gut as dietary fibre.

answers.text: Glycogen contains fructose units that are more easily hydrolysed than the glucose units in cellulose

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both glycogen and cellulose are composed entirely of glucose, not fructose. The critical difference is the bond type — alpha glycosidic bonds in glycogen are cleaved by human amylases, while beta bonds in cellulose are not.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key difference is the glycosidic bond type. Glycogen has alpha-1,4 bonds cleaved by amylase, while cellulose has beta-1,4 bonds that humans lack the enzyme (cellulase) to break. This is why cellulose acts as indigestible fibre.
Correct. Cellulose has beta glycosidic bonds that human enzymes cannot cleave, so it passes through the gut as dietary fibre. Glycogen has alpha bonds that amylase readily hydrolyses.

interactions.label: Oral rehydration salts (ORS) contain glucose as an essential component. Which in

params.question: Oral rehydration salts (ORS) contain glucose as an essential component. Which intestinal transporter explains why glucose enhances water absorption in ORS therapy?

answers.text: GLUT-2, which transports glucose across the basolateral membrane of enterocytes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: GLUT-2 operates at the basolateral side to move glucose into the blood, but it does not couple glucose with sodium. ORS works because SGLT-1 at the apical brush border co-transports glucose and sodium, creating an osmotic gradient that draws water into the cell.

answers.text: GLUT-4, which is activated by insulin to allow glucose uptake

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: GLUT-4 operates in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, not in the intestinal epithelium. ORS therapy relies on SGLT-1, the sodium-dependent glucose transporter at the intestinal brush border, which couples glucose and sodium uptake and draws water osmotically.

answers.text: SGLT-1, which co-transports glucose and sodium across the intestinal epithelium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. SGLT-1 at the apical brush border couples glucose and sodium uptake via secondary active transport, powered by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase gradient. Water follows osmotically. This is precisely why glucose is an essential ingredient in ORS — without it, sodium and water absorption is much less efficient.

answers.text: GLUT-5, which facilitates fructose absorption by passive diffusion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: GLUT-5 transports fructose, not glucose, and uses facilitated diffusion without sodium coupling. ORS relies on SGLT-1, which co-transports glucose with sodium — the coupled sodium movement creates the osmotic force that pulls water across the intestinal wall.

overallFeedback.feedback: ORS works through SGLT-1, the sodium-dependent glucose transporter at the intestinal brush border. It couples glucose and sodium absorption via secondary active transport. Water follows the sodium gradient osmotically — this is why glucose is an essential component of ORS.
Correct. SGLT-1 co-transports sodium and glucose at the brush border, and water follows osmotically. This is the physiological basis of oral rehydration therapy.

params.question: Red blood cells depend entirely on glycolysis for ATP production. Which structural feature of mature red blood cells explains this complete dependence?

answers.text: They lack a cell membrane Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Red blood cells do possess Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase — it is essential for maintaining their biconcave shape. Their exclusive dependence on glycolysis is because they lack mitochondria and therefore cannot perform oxidative phosphorylation or the TCA cycle.

answers.text: They lack mitochondria

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Mature red blood cells have no mitochondria. Without mitochondria, they cannot run the TCA cycle or the electron transport chain. Cytoplasmic glycolysis is therefore their sole source of ATP, yielding a net of 2 ATP per glucose molecule.

answers.text: They lack hexokinase, the first glycolytic enzyme

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Red blood cells do contain hexokinase and all other glycolytic enzymes — that is precisely why they can perform glycolysis. Their exclusive reliance on this pathway is because they lack mitochondria for oxidative phosphorylation.

answers.text: They lack GLUT transporters and cannot take up glucose efficiently

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Red blood cells express GLUT-1, which provides continuous, insulin-independent glucose uptake. Their reliance on glycolysis is not a glucose supply issue — it is because they lack mitochondria, making glycolysis the only pathway available for ATP generation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Mature red blood cells lack mitochondria entirely. Without mitochondria, neither the TCA cycle nor oxidative phosphorylation can operate. Glycolysis — running in the cytoplasm — is therefore their sole source of ATP, yielding a net 2 ATP per glucose.
Correct. Without mitochondria, red blood cells cannot run the TCA cycle or oxidative phosphorylation. Glycolysis in the cytoplasm is their only ATP source.

interactions.label: Fatty acids can serve as precursors for gluconeogenesis in the liver.

params.question: Fatty acids can serve as precursors for gluconeogenesis in the liver.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Fatty acids are broken down to acetyl-CoA via beta-oxidation, but acetyl-CoA cannot re-enter gluconeogenesis because the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is irreversible (it only converts pyruvate → acetyl-CoA, never the reverse). The valid gluconeogenic precursors are lactate (Cori cycle), glycerol (from fat breakdown), and glucogenic amino acids (especially alanine). This explains why prolonged starvation causes muscle protein breakdown.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Fatty acids are oxidised to acetyl-CoA, but acetyl-CoA cannot be converted back to pyruvate because the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is irreversible. Only lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids can serve as gluconeogenic precursors. This is why prolonged starvation causes muscle wasting — the body must break down protein to maintain blood glucose, since fat alone cannot do this.

interactions.label: A newborn develops cataracts and liver damage shortly after starting breast milk

params.question: A newborn develops cataracts and liver damage shortly after starting breast milk feeds. Deficiency of which enzyme is the most likely cause?

answers.text: Aldolase B

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aldolase B deficiency causes hereditary fructose intolerance, which presents after introduction of fruits or sucrose-containing foods, not with milk feeds. The presentation here — cataracts and liver damage triggered by milk — points to galactosaemia, caused by deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyl transferase.

answers.text: Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyl transferase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This is classic galactosaemia. Breast milk contains lactose, which is hydrolysed to glucose and galactose. Without this transferase, galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in the lens (cataracts), liver (damage), and brain (intellectual disability). Treatment requires complete elimination of lactose from the diet.

answers.text: Aldose reductase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol in the polyol pathway. Its overactivity in chronic hyperglycaemia (diabetes) causes complications such as cataracts and neuropathy, but this occurs in diabetics, not in neonates on breast milk. The presentation here fits galactosaemia.

answers.text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: G6PD deficiency causes haemolytic anaemia triggered by oxidative stress — drugs like primaquine, sulfonamides, fava beans, or infections. It does not cause cataracts and liver damage in neonates on milk feeds. This presentation fits classic galactosaemia from galactose-1-phosphate uridylyl transferase deficiency.

overallFeedback.feedback: This is classic galactosaemia, caused by deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyl transferase. Breast milk contains lactose, which yields galactose upon digestion. Without the transferase, galactose-1-phosphate accumulates, causing cataracts, liver damage, and intellectual disability. Treatment is complete dietary lactose elimination.

Correct. Classic galactosaemia results from galactose-1-phosphate uridylyl transferase deficiency. Lactose in breast milk is the source of galactose, and its accumulation damages the lens, liver, and brain.

interactions.label: HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over 2–3 months. In which of the following

params.question: HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over 2–3 months. In which of the following conditions would HbA1c give a misleadingly low result?

answers.text: Iron deficiency anaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Iron deficiency anaemia does not shorten red blood cell lifespan. HbA1c is misleadingly low when red cells are destroyed prematurely — as in haemolytic anaemia — because younger replacement cells have had less time to accumulate glycated haemoglobin.

answers.text: Hypothyroidism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hypothyroidism does not significantly alter red blood cell survival. HbA1c becomes falsely low when the red cell lifespan is shortened, as in haemolytic anaemia, sickle cell disease, or after recent blood transfusions — younger cells carry less glycated haemoglobin.

answers.text: Haemolytic anaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. HbA1c depends on glucose binding irreversibly to haemoglobin over the red cell's ~120-day lifespan. In haemolytic anaemia, red cells are destroyed prematurely and replaced by younger cells that have had less time to glycate. This gives a falsely low HbA1c, potentially masking poor glucose control.

answers.text: Chronic kidney disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chronic kidney disease does not typically shorten red cell lifespan in a way that lowers HbA1c. A misleadingly low HbA1c occurs when red blood cell turnover is accelerated — as in haemolytic anaemia, sickle cell disease, or after recent blood transfusions — because younger cells carry less glycated haemoglobin.

overallFeedback.feedback: HbA1c measures glucose permanently bound to haemoglobin over the red cell's ~120-day lifespan. When that lifespan is shortened — in haemolytic anaemia, sickle cell disease, or after transfusion — younger replacement cells carry less glycated haemoglobin, producing a misleadingly low reading.
Correct. Haemolytic anaemia shortens red blood cell lifespan, so haemoglobin has less time to accumulate glucose. This gives a falsely low HbA1c, potentially masking true glycaemic status.
